narrative:
The model estimated a 61.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because your law school application was evaluated with that prediction, the projected risk was high enough that your application was denied.

Of the factors behind this prediction, your third-year class rank mattered most. You were in the second decile, well below the accepted-student average of about the sixth decile, and this strongly pushed the prediction toward bar-exam failure. Your LSAT score was the next most influential factor: at 37, it was essentially at the accepted-student average of 37.18, and in your case it pushed slightly toward passing. Your first-year rank was the third most important factor; at the third decile versus an accepted average of about the sixth decile, it also pushed toward failure. Although the LSAT signal was favorable, the two low class-rank signals outweighed it. Family income and full-time status were not among the top drivers.

Next, ask admissions whether you may reapply and what evidence would strengthen a future file. Focus on raising your LSAT if feasible, taking rigorous coursework or a post-baccalaureate program to show academic improvement, and gaining legal or paralegal experience that demonstrates readiness. A stronger recent academic record and test score are the most direct ways to reduce the predicted bar-exam risk before reapplying.
